findings.reason: The protected JavaScript solution implements function currying using immutable linked nodes ({ previous, values: nextArgs }) to track argument batches without premature array copying. When accumulated argument count reaches fn.length, it flattens nodes in reverse order and evaluates fn(...args). The currying implementation runs in O(n + p) time and O(n + p) space; no candidate is required.

Immutable node chains ensure partial curry state can be safely reused across multiple branches. Flattening linked nodes in reverse order reconstructs original argument order exactly. Zero-parameter functions (fn.length == 0) trigger immediate evaluation upon invocation.

Across p calls supplying n total arguments, node creation takes O(n + p) time and the final flattening pass takes O(n + p) time. Space complexity is O(n + p) for linked nodes and arguments. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts function fn, returning a curried function wrapper that collects arguments until fn.length is met and evaluates fn.

The approach accurately details immutable linked node argument collection, deferred flattening at arity completion, zero-arity handling, and O(n + p) time / O(n + p) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover array copy overhead, shared mutable accumulator risks, Function.prototype.bind limitations, empty argument batches, zero arity, argument order preservation, and reusable partial curries.

App JavaScript and native JavaScript solutions both execute the identical linked-node currying closure algorithm with SHA-256 digests 5cf307da57a18dcc42a2210407424cea1d56d020295669bf2c11723665160a98 and 3e1bfde8dbb0e2f11e6e094e89bfeef9ae15152f646dabcaef50af2ef4f6d409.
